title: MCPdia
summary: Long-term memory for LLMs: a knowledge graph of linked notes served over MCP, so a model finds one answer without rereading whole files.
body:
MCPdia stands for Model Context Protocol: Distilled, Indexed Answers. It gives LLMs a memory that lasts between sessions and can be shared by a team.

Tell your LLM "remember this" once, and it finds the answer later without rereading whole files. MCPdia stores what you know as linked nodes. It hands the model small summaries first and lets the model decide what is worth reading in full. The model does the filing too: it writes, links and corrects nodes as it works.

The point is saving tokens. Memory kept in markdown files gets read in full every time, and the cost grows with the files. With MCPdia, reading one answer costs about the same at 80 facts or 1,600.

- Open source, MIT licensed: https://github.com/bradwagoner/mcpdia
- Works with Claude Code and any MCP client, over stdio or HTTP.
- Runs locally on SQLite with no setup, or as one shared Postgres server for a team.
aliases: model context protocol: distilled, indexed answers
author: local

title: How MCPdia works
summary: Stubs first, read only what matters, follow links, write back as you go, nothing is lost, and feedback on what helped.
body:
MCPdia keeps memory cheap to read and easy to keep current. Six ideas do the work:

- Stubs first: search returns one line per node, not whole files.
- Render levels: read a node at title, summary, snippet or full.
- Links: related facts sit one hop away.
- Write back as you go: tools are named for what the model wants to do, and the server does the bookkeeping.
- Nothing is lost: edits are versioned, deletes are soft, and replaced facts point to their replacement.
- Feedback: models mark nodes useful, not useful or wrong.

The code has three layers. Thin MCP tools sit on a core that holds every rule, and the core sits on a storage interface with SQLite and Postgres behind it.
author: local

title: Using MCPdia
summary: How to install MCPdia, run it in Docker, use it day to day, seed it with an LLM, export it, and measure your token use.
body:
Start with the install guide (Node, about two minutes), or the Docker guide for a shared server. Then:

- Day to day: say "remember this", ask questions, and let the model file what it learns.
- Seeding: point an LLM at your docs or repo and have it build the graph for you.
- Export: the whole graph as one JSONL file.
- Measuring: turn on the metrics log to see where a session's tokens went.
author: local

title: MCPdia tools
summary: Twelve MCP tools named for intent: orient, search, get, upsert, annotate, link, supersede, verify, delete, feedback, recent, list_types.
body:
Each tool covers one intent and has a short description, because descriptions load every session. Results are compact plain text, not JSON.

When a tool knows something the caller would want, the result says it in one line: the fact, then the next step. Examples are a partial search match, a node flagged as wrong, a link left dangling, or a new node with no parent. Hints never block a call.

In Claude Code the tools load on demand. Until the model needs MCPdia, a session carries only the tool names.

Full reference: https://github.com/bradwagoner/mcpdia/blob/main/docs/tools.md
author: local

title: MCPdia results
summary: Measured: every task right at 44% less cost than one big memory file, answers stay findable at 100,000 nodes, and the cost of an answer stays flat.
body:
Every number comes from benches in the repo that anyone can rerun:

- Live Claude sessions: 20/20 tasks right at $0.0027 per session, 44% less than one CLAUDE.md.
- Lookups at scale: the answer is in the top 3 for 38 to 40 of 40 questions, from 82 to 100,082 nodes.
- Flat cost per answer: about 660 tokens per answer, while one markdown file grows from 15,000 to 250,000 tokens.
- SQLite vs Postgres: both find the same nodes. SQLite is quickest for one person, and Postgres keeps up with many clients.
author: local

title: MCPdia design decisions
summary: The 25 decision records behind MCPdia: what was chosen, why, and what was given up.
body:
Every significant choice is written down at the time it is made and never rewritten. When a decision changes, a new record supersedes the old one, and the old one stays as history. Each decision node links to the feature it shaped.

Source files: https://github.com/bradwagoner/mcpdia/tree/main/docs/decisions
author: local

title: Sharing MCPdia with a team
summary: One shared Docker/Postgres server that everyone connects to over HTTP; register your own local graph beside it to keep private notes private.
body:
A team shares one graph by running one MCPdia server. `docker compose up -d` starts Postgres, the server on port 7411 and the read-only viewer on port 7412. Each person registers it once:

claude mcp add --transport http mcpdia http://localhost:7411/mcp

From then on, what one person's LLM learns, everyone's LLM can find. Notes are separate nodes per author, so two people commenting on the same thing never collide. Edits to the same node are protected by a version check.

To keep your own notes private, register your local server too, under another name. Each MCP server is its own tool set, so your model can read both graphs and choose where to write.

Today the HTTP server answers localhost only, and there is no login. Run it on one machine or a network you trust. Token auth and per-namespace permissions are next on the roadmap (v0.3).
author: local

title: MCPdia graph viewer
summary: A read-only browser view of the graph: search, click a node to see its details and neighbors, and watch it update live as LLMs write.
body:
The viewer lets you see what your LLMs have written. You can:

- Search.
- Click a node to see its details, neighbors and siblings.
- Hide unrelated nodes while one is selected.
- Read a legend of node and edge types.

It renders with Sigma.js (WebGL) by default, with Cytoscape.js as an option. It handles thousands of nodes.

It opens the database read-only and answers on localhost. With Docker it runs at http://localhost:7412 and follows the graph live as clients write. It lives in viewer/, with its own package.json, so the server install stays lean.
author: local

title: MCPdia security
summary: Stored text is data, not instructions; by default MCPdia runs locally over stdio with no network port, and the HTTP server answers localhost only.
body:
MCPdia hands stored text back to LLMs, so treat what it returns as data, not instructions. A node can inform an agent, never authorize it. The server's MCP instructions say so at the start of every session. The real safeguard is the client's own confirmation step before an agent acts.

- Default: stdio, a SQLite file in your home folder, no network port and no outbound requests.
- HTTP and Docker: listens on 127.0.0.1, answers only local host names (which blocks DNS rebinding), and Postgres is not published.
- Audit trail: every write is stamped and versioned, and nothing is hard-deleted. A bad node can be flagged, superseded or deleted, and the original stays on record.
- Keep secrets out of the graph: there is no per-node access control, and history is never purged.

Details: https://github.com/bradwagoner/mcpdia/blob/main/SECURITY.md
author: local

title: MCPdia roadmap
summary: v0.2 brings cleanup tools, JSONL import and seeding from a document or repo; v0.3 adds token auth, per-namespace permissions and an AWS deployment.
body:
- v0.1 (done): twelve tools, SQLite with full-text search, JSONL export, the metrics log, the graph viewer, and CI on Linux, macOS and Windows. Postgres, HTTP and the Docker image shipped early.
- v0.2, cleanup and packs: finders for duplicate and stale nodes, bulk merges and renames with dry runs, JSONL import, and seeding a graph from a document or repo.
- v0.3, team mode: token auth, per-namespace permissions and a documented AWS deployment.

Release diary: https://github.com/bradwagoner/mcpdia/blob/main/docs/SCOPE.md
author: local

title: Stubs first
summary: Search returns one compact line per node, so the model reads a few hundred tokens instead of a whole file before choosing what to open.
body:
A search result is a stub: key, type and title, plus a one-line summary or the snippet around the match. A stub looks like this:

concept/permissions [concept] Permission system
  Roles grant actions; groups hold roles. · 4 links

Responses are plain text with no JSON field names. That makes the same stub about 37% shorter. When a searched word sits deep in a long body, the snippet shows the text around it, so the fact is often in the stub itself.
author: local

title: Render levels
summary: Every read picks how much to return: title, summary, snippet or full, so the cheap path is the default path.
body:
- title: key, type and title.
- summary: adds the one-line summary, link count and last-verified date.
- snippet: adds about 300 characters of the body, or the text around the match.
- full: adds the whole body, tags, aliases and properties.

Defaults: summary for search, title for neighbors, and full for a get by key. Callers can predict the cost of every call.
author: local

title: Links between nodes
summary: Nodes link to their parents and to each other with typed edges (part_of, depends_on, references...), so related facts are one hop away.
body:
Each node has a readable key such as concept/permissions. Edges are typed and free-form. The common ones are part_of, related_to, depends_on, references, supersedes and comments_on. `get` with neighbors lists linked nodes as titles, so the model can follow a trail without loading it.

Edges store the key at each end, not a row id. A link can point at a node that doesn't exist yet, or that lives in another namespace, and it resolves when that node arrives. That is what makes import and partial loads safe.
author: local

title: Write back as you go
summary: The model files what it learns with tools named for intent (upsert, annotate, link, supersede, verify); the server does the bookkeeping.
body:
There are no hand-kept index files. The model writes while it works:

- upsert creates or corrects a fact, and links it under its parent in the same call.
- annotate leaves a note as its own linked node, so the original stays clean.
- supersede replaces an outdated fact and moves its links.
- verify marks a fact as checked.

Shared facts live in the node, and observations live in notes. Types are free-form. New ones are pointed out, never blocked.
author: local

title: Nothing is lost
summary: Every edit is versioned, deletes are soft and can be undone, and a superseded fact points to its replacement.
body:
- Each change to a node's content or status keeps a snapshot of the old version.
- delete is a soft delete. `get` and `search` with all_status show deleted nodes, and writing to a deleted key restores it.
- supersede keeps the old fact as history and marks it "superseded by" the new one, at every read level. A model never mistakes an old fact for a current one.

If something turns out wrong or out of date, flag it with feedback, supersede it, or restore an earlier node. Nothing is gone for good.
author: local

title: Feedback on nodes
summary: Models mark nodes useful, not useful or outdated_or_wrong; useful nodes rank a little higher, and wrong ones are flagged on every read until fixed.
body:
The feedback tool turns every LLM that uses the graph into a staleness detector. Verdicts are stored as counters on the node:

- useful: a small search boost (at most 10%), and the node shows in `recent`.
- not_useful: a cleanup signal.
- outdated_or_wrong: `search` and `get` show "(flagged outdated or wrong)" until someone edits or verifies the node.

Reads are never tracked. Only real verdicts count.
author: local

title: orient tool
summary: The welcome mat: a few hundred tokens on what this graph is, its house rules and where to start; optional focus words add likely-relevant titles.
body:
Call it first in a session. It returns:

- What the graph is.
- The working loop: search, read stubs, expand, write back, give feedback.
- Team house rules.
- Node counts and the top types.
- Pinned "start here" nodes.

Pass `focus` with a few words about the task to get up to 5 matching titles. The intro, rules, pins and size preset (minimal, standard, verbose) are settings, so a team can change them without code.
author: local

title: search tool
summary: Keyword search over titles, summaries, bodies, aliases and tags; returns short stubs ranked by relevance, with partial matches labelled.
body:
Search runs on full-text search: FTS5 on SQLite, or tsvector on Postgres. It matches word stems and drops question words. The title weighs most.

Nodes that match every word come first. When there are fewer of them than the limit, nodes that match some words fill the rest, each labelled with the words it matched. The header says how many full and partial matches there are.

Filter by `type` or `tag`, pick a render level, and set `all_status` to include history.
author: local

title: get tool
summary: Fetch up to 10 nodes by key at any render level, optionally with their linked nodes as titles.
body:
`get` takes a list of keys and defaults to the full level. Set `neighbors` to list linked nodes, grouped by direction and edge type, capped at 20.

A missing key says "Not found" and points to search. A deleted key says it was deleted. A superseded node names its replacement.
author: local

title: upsert tool
summary: Create a node, or edit its own facts by key, and link it under its parent in the same call.
body:
Leave out the key to create a node. The key is built from the type and title, for example how-to/granting-admin-access. If that key already belongs to a live node, the write stops and names it: search before write, built in.

`links` adds edges in the same call. A new node with no parent gets a one-line hint. A `version` check guards against two writers editing at once. Writing to a deleted key restores that node.
author: local

title: annotate tool
summary: Leave a note on a node; it is saved as its own linked note node, and the original node is unchanged.
body: One call creates a note node with a readable key, the author and a comments_on edge to the target. The target's body and version don't change. Notes from different people never collide, and shared nodes don't bloat with appended comments.
author: local

title: link tool
summary: Link two nodes with a typed edge such as depends_on, part_of, references or related_to; the target may not exist yet.
body:
Edge types are normalized to snake_case. Linking the same pair with the same type again updates the edge's note.

The result warns when the target is deleted or superseded, or when a parent edge would make a loop.
author: local

title: supersede tool
summary: Replace an outdated node with a new one; its links move to the replacement and the old node stays as history.
body: The old node is marked superseded and points at its replacement. A supersedes edge keeps the history visible. Reads of the old node say "superseded by <key>" at every level, so an old fact never passes as current.
author: local

title: verify tool
summary: Mark nodes as checked and still correct; sets the verified date shown at summary level and clears a wrong flag.
body: Takes up to 50 keys. It doesn't create a version. The "verified" date appears on summary stubs, so readers can tell a fresh fact from an old one.
author: local

title: delete tool
summary: Soft-delete nodes: they leave normal reads but keep their history, and writing to the key restores them.
body: Takes up to 50 keys. The result lists live nodes that still link to a deleted one, since those links now lead nowhere. If something replaces the node, use supersede instead.
author: local

title: feedback tool
summary: Say which nodes helped: useful, not_useful or outdated_or_wrong.
body: Takes up to 50 keys and one verdict. useful gives a small search boost and shows in recent. outdated_or_wrong flags the node on every read until someone edits or verifies it.
author: local

title: recent tool
summary: Latest changes and nodes marked useful, newest first; filter by your own writes or a time span such as 3d.
body: This is the quickest way to pick up where a previous session left off. It tracks writes and useful marks, never reads. An empty result names its filters.
author: local

title: list_types tool
summary: Node and edge types in use, with counts; check it before inventing a type, and it points out look-alikes such as concept and concepts.
body: Types are free-form strings. Only case, whitespace and separators are normalized. list_types makes the vocabulary visible so models reuse it instead of drifting into ticket, Ticket and jira-ticket. New types are allowed and pointed out, never blocked.
author: local

title: Install MCPdia
summary: Needs Node 22+, no clone and no build tools: one npx command registers it with your MCP client.
body:
Register it with Claude Code:
claude mcp add mcpdia -- npx -y @bradwagoner/mcpdia

That's the whole install: npx fetches the package the first time the server starts. Put the server name before any -e KEY=VALUE flags. The tools appear in your next session.

Other stdio MCP clients (Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code) use the same command in their MCP config: command npx, arguments -y and @bradwagoner/mcpdia. For a shared server over HTTP, use the Docker guide.

The graph lives in ~/.mcpdia/mcpdia.db. Set MCPDIA_DB to keep it somewhere else. The SQLite driver ships prebuilt for Windows, macOS and Linux, so you don't need Visual Studio or other build tools.

To run from source instead:
git clone https://github.com/bradwagoner/mcpdia.git
cd mcpdia
npm install
npm run build
claude mcp add mcpdia -- node /path/to/mcpdia/dist/index.js
author: local

title: Run MCPdia in Docker
summary: One command starts Postgres, the MCPdia server on port 7411 and the live graph viewer on port 7412; or use the SQLite compose file for one machine.
body:
docker compose up -d
claude mcp add --transport http mcpdia http://localhost:7411/mcp

That's MCPdia on Postgres 17, serving every client from one graph, with the viewer at http://localhost:7412. The graph lives in the pgdata volume and survives rebuilds.

Prefer a single SQLite file? Run docker compose -f docker-compose.sqlite.yml up -d. Run one stack at a time, since both use the same ports.

Set POSTGRES_PASSWORD before the first start. Everything is published on 127.0.0.1 only. All settings: https://github.com/bradwagoner/mcpdia/blob/main/docs/docker.md
author: local

title: Use MCPdia day to day
summary: Say "remember this" and the model files it; ask a question and it searches stubs, then reads only the node that answers.
body:
You talk to your LLM as usual. MCPdia works underneath:

- "Remember that staging deploys need a VPN." The model searches first, then upserts a node under the right parent.
- "How do we deploy to staging?" The model searches, reads the summary stubs, and gets the one node that answers, instead of rereading every notes file.
- "That's out of date, it's Tailscale now." The model supersedes the old fact. The old one stays as history and points to the new one.
- "Note that this broke for Sam last week." The model annotates the node, and the note becomes its own linked node.
- At the start of a session, orient and recent show what's there and what changed.

The model also marks which nodes helped with feedback, so good answers rise and wrong ones get flagged.
author: local

title: Seed a graph with an LLM
summary: Point your LLM at existing docs, a repo or your old markdown notes and ask it to file them into MCPdia as linked nodes; nobody builds the graph by hand.
body:
You don't have to start from empty. Ask your model something like:

"Read docs/ and CLAUDE.md. File each fact, decision and how-to into MCPdia as its own node, one thing per node, under a parent topic, with links between related nodes. Search before you write so you don't make duplicates."

The model uses the same tools it uses every day: upsert with links, link and annotate. A team can do this once against the shared server, and from then on everyone's LLM starts with the team's knowledge.

Today the model does the seeding through the tools. A built-in "seed from a document or repo" command is on the v0.2 roadmap.
author: local

title: Export the graph
summary: node dist/index.js export --out graph.jsonl writes active nodes and their links as JSON Lines, for backup or moving a graph.
body:
node dist/index.js export --out graph.jsonl

- Add --namespace ns to pick namespaces.
- Add --all-status to include superseded and deleted nodes.
- In Docker: docker compose exec -T mcpdia node dist/index.js export > graph.jsonl

Nodes carry a stable (namespace, key) identity, so an export can be matched up again later. JSONL import is on the v0.2 roadmap. The format is described in docs/schema.md.
author: local

title: Measure your token use
summary: Set MCPDIA_METRICS=1 and every tool call adds one line of measured facts (tool, ms, request and response size) to mcpdia-metrics.jsonl.
body:
claude mcp add mcpdia -e MCPDIA_METRICS=1 -- node /path/to/mcpdia/dist/index.js

Each call writes a line such as:
{"ts":"2026-10-19T15:40:02.114Z","session":"01K7…","tool":"search","ms":4,"ok":true,"req_chars":38,"res_chars":912,"level":"summary"}

The line holds only measured values: no estimates, no query text, no node content. Pair it with Claude's own usage report (claude -p --output-format json) to see where a session's tokens went, request by request. It's off by default. Delete the file to start over.
author: local

title: Result: live Claude sessions
summary: Same tasks, fresh sessions: MCPdia got 20/20 right at $0.0027 per session, 44% less than one big CLAUDE.md (20/20, $0.0049).
body:
Three ways to keep memory, the same questions, the same facts, and fresh Claude sessions:

| Memory | Tasks done right | Cost per session |
|---|---|---|
| MCPdia | 20/20 | $0.0027 |
| One CLAUDE.md with everything in it | 20/20 | $0.0049 |
| A CLAUDE.md index plus hand-split topic files | 19/20 | $0.0022 |

Every task was right, at 44% less cost than one big memory file. Hand-split markdown comes close on cost, but someone has to keep the index and topic files in order. With MCPdia, the model files what it learns as it goes.

Method: Claude Haiku 5.5, ten read and write tasks against a fictional product team's knowledge (82 facts), each run twice, with every session starting from a fresh copy. Rerun it from bench/sessions. Every session's pass, cost and tokens are in sessions.csv.
author: local

title: Result: answers stay findable at scale
summary: 40 questions with the answers hidden among generated nodes: the answer is in the top 3 for 38 to 40 of them from 82 to 100,082 nodes, and get stays under a millisecond.
body:
| Nodes | Answer in the top 3 | Search p50 / p95 | Get p50 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 82 | 39/40 | 2.0 / 3.3 ms | 0.1 ms |
| 1,082 | 40/40 | 2.3 / 3.9 ms | 0.1 ms |
| 10,082 | 39/40 | 9.6 / 22 ms | 0.2 ms |
| 100,082 | 38/40 | 339 / 755 ms | 0.2 ms |

Measured on a Windows desktop with no model involved, so it costs nothing to rerun: npm run bench:lookups. The same checks run on every npm test, with floors set to today's scores, so a search regression shows up right away.
author: local

title: Result: the cost of an answer stays flat
summary: Reading one answer from MCPdia takes about 660 tokens at 82 facts or 1,600; loading the same memory as one markdown file grows from 15,000 to 250,000 tokens.
body:
This is the core of the token story. Markdown memory is read whole, so its cost grows with everything you've ever written down. MCPdia reads stubs, then one node, so the cost of an answer barely moves as memory grows.

| Memory size | MCPdia per answer | One markdown file |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 82 facts | ~660 tokens | ~15,000 tokens |
| 1,600 facts | ~660 tokens | ~250,000 tokens |

Rerun it with npm run bench:growth. The full per-size series is in bench/growth.json, ready to chart.
author: local

title: Result: SQLite or Postgres
summary: Both stores find the same nodes (177 and 176 of 177 in the top 3); SQLite is quickest for one person, Postgres keeps up when many clients share a big graph.
body:
Both Docker stacks on one machine, over HTTP, first with a real 177-node graph and then with 10,000 more nodes:

| | SQLite | Postgres | SQLite +10k | Postgres +10k |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Search, 1 client, p50 | 32 ms | 39 ms | 81 ms | 121 ms |
| Get, 1 client, p50 | 15 ms | 15 ms | 15 ms | 15 ms |
| 16 clients, 1 write in 4 | 144 calls/s | 56 calls/s | 23 calls/s | 77 calls/s |

On a big shared graph with many writers, Postgres handles over three times the calls of SQLite. Rerun with npm run bench:stores. Your numbers will differ with your machine, but the shape holds.
author: local

title: ADR 0001: TypeScript and a three-layer architecture
summary: TypeScript, with thin MCP tools over a core that holds every rule, over an async storage interface, so storage and transport can change without touching the rules.
body:
Context: the same logic has to serve one person with zero setup and, later, a team on shared infrastructure.

Decision: build in TypeScript, in three layers. MCP tools are thin adapters. The core holds the rules (search before write, type normalization, versioning, render levels) and knows nothing about MCP or storage. GraphStore is an async storage interface, with SQLite first and Postgres second. Every core call takes a context object (caller, namespaces).

Passed over: Python with FastMCP, since the MCP ecosystem and one-line installs favor TypeScript. Also a single script, which would make team mode a rewrite.

Trade-offs: a store can be swapped without touching tools or rules, and one test suite runs against both stores. Everything is async, even where SQLite doesn't need it.
author: local

title: ADR 0002: Free-form types with soft guardrails
summary: Node and edge types are free-form strings, normalized only for case and separators; list_types shows the vocabulary, and new types are pointed out, never blocked.
body:
Context: every domain needs its own types, but LLM writers drift (ticket, Ticket, jira-ticket), and searches then miss most of them.

Decision: types are free-form strings. Only case, whitespace and separators are normalized. list_types shows types with counts. A new type is allowed and pointed out. A small starter vocabulary is offered as suggestions, not rules. Drift is handled with detection and reversible cleanup, not prevention.

Passed over: hard-coded enums, which are too rigid. Also auto-merging look-alike types, which can be wrong.

Trade-offs: maximum flexibility, and some drift is accepted. ADR 0018 later replaced the "did you mean?" guess with a plain fact.
author: local

title: ADR 0003: Stable keys, namespaces and portable packs
summary: ULIDs for internal ids, a readable (namespace, key) as the identity across graphs, soft delete, and a portable JSONL export so graphs can be shared and merged later.
body:
Context: importing curated packs, merging datasets and promoting personal notes to a shared graph only work if two graphs can tell that two rows are the same thing.

Decision: ULIDs for internal references. A stable key such as concept/permission-system, unique per namespace, as the identity across graphs. Every row carries namespace, source, author, timestamps and a version. Soft delete through status. JSONL export as a first-class feature. Namespaces are the subset mechanism.

Passed over: auto-increment ids, which collide across instances. Also content hashes, which break on edit.

Trade-offs: the columns exist from day one, ready for import, merge and auth.
author: local

title: ADR 0004: Render levels and a lean, configurable orient
summary: Every read picks title, summary, snippet or full, defaulting to the cheap level; orient stays a few hundred tokens and is configured by settings.
body:
Context: the project exists to save tokens. Anything that returns more than the caller needs defeats the purpose.

Decision: one render-level enum for every read tool. Defaults: summary for search, title for neighbors, full for a get by key. orient is the welcome mat: what this is, the working loop, house rules, counts, pinned nodes and optional focus results. It's built from settings in layers (defaults, pack, team, personal). recent tracks writes and useful marks, never reads.

Passed over: a token budget, which is unpredictable. Also listing every type by default, and read tracking.

Trade-offs: callers can predict cost, and the cheap path is the default.
author: local

title: ADR 0005: Usefulness feedback as a separate tool
summary: A feedback tool with useful, not_useful and outdated_or_wrong, stored as counters; a small ranking boost and a staleness signal, instead of read counts.
body:
Context: read counts measure curiosity and turn every read into a write. What matters is whether a node helped, or turned out wrong.

Decision: a dedicated feedback tool. Counters and a last-useful timestamp live on the node. Useful gives a small search boost and shows in recent. outdated_or_wrong makes every LLM a staleness detector. The tool is nudged in orient and in its own description.

Passed over: an optional useful_ids parameter on other tools, which muddies them. Also read counts.

Trade-offs: the signal is soft, so the boost stays small.
author: local

title: ADR 0006: One codebase, user-chosen deployment mode
summary: The same project runs solo (SQLite over stdio) or as a team server (HTTP and Postgres in Docker); a central server is the team model, not peer-to-peer sync.
body:
Context: a developer should be able to try it in minutes, then take the same project to their team and company infrastructure without switching tools.

Decision: one codebase with three modes. Solo is a local SQLite file over stdio. Solo plus seed imports a pack at setup. Team runs the same core behind HTTP in Docker on Postgres. A central server is the team model. Auth comes later, and the context object is ready for it.

Passed over: federated or peer-to-peer sync, where conflicts, identity and trust cost more than they give. Also key-value stores, which suit graph traversal and text search poorly.

Trade-offs: two storage adapters kept honest by one shared test suite. Optimistic concurrency through a version column.
author: local

title: ADR 0007: Late-bound edges and ghost nodes
summary: Edges store namespace + key for both ends, with resolved ids filled in when the node exists, so links can point at nodes not loaded yet.
body:
Context: foreign-key edges can't exist unless both ends are loaded. That breaks partial loads, import ordering and links across packs.

Decision: an edge's real reference is the namespace and key at each end. from_id and to_id are nullable shortcuts, resolved when the node appears. Later, a traversal that hits an unloaded end returns a collapsed "ghost" with a hint on which pack to load.

Passed over: forbidding cross-namespace edges, dropping edges on partial load, or inserting placeholder rows.

Trade-offs: four extra columns and a resolve step. Multi-dataset support stays cheap: context.namespaces is a list.
author: local

title: ADR 0008: Intent-named tools and separate note nodes
summary: Shared facts live in the node and observations in linked note nodes; tools are named for intent (annotate, supersede, verify) and the core does the bookkeeping.
body:
Context: two people commenting on the same ticket shouldn't collide, and an LLM shouldn't bloat a shared node by appending notes to it.

Decision: users are not part of the key. Each comment is its own note node with the author and a comments_on edge. Edits to the same node are guarded by a version check. Tools are named for intent: annotate, supersede, verify, upsert. Guidance lives in tool descriptions, not in write-time limits. Mistakes are fixed by cleanup, not prevented. There's no fixed cap on tools, but no near-duplicates.

Passed over: generic CRUD with many options. Also user-scoped keys, and growth warnings at write time.

Trade-offs: leaving a note is one call and cheaper than editing a body, so it's the path of least resistance.
author: local

title: ADR 0009: Project name MCPedia (superseded)
summary: The first name, MCPedia, was kept despite an unrelated project of the same name; superseded by ADR 0022, which renamed the project MCPdia.
body:
Context: the project needed a memorable name that says what it is. Cairn, Mycelium, Knot, Gnode, Noted and Lexigraph were considered. MCPedia (MCP plus encyclopedia) won, but an unrelated project with that name existed in the same niche.

Decision at the time: use MCPedia anyway, under the author's own GitHub and npm scope, and revisit before the first public release.

What happened: ADR 0022 revisited it and renamed the project MCPdia.
author: local

title: ADR 0010: SQLite library: better-sqlite3
summary: better-sqlite3: stable, FTS5 built in, and prebuilt binaries for Windows, macOS and Linux, so installs need no build tools.
body:
Context: search needs SQLite's FTS5, and the install must work cleanly on every OS.

Decision: better-sqlite3 13. It's the long-standing default, ships its own SQLite with FTS5, and uses N-API prebuilt binaries, so npm install never runs node-gyp. This was verified on Windows without Visual Studio. Its sync calls are wrapped in the async GraphStore.

Passed over: node:sqlite, the runner-up, which is still experimental on current LTS releases and prints a warning. Switching later touches one file. Also libsql, which is in maintenance mode.

Trade-offs: one native dependency, and FTS5 behaves the same everywhere. Needs Node 22 or later.
author: local

title: ADR 0011: Compact text responses
summary: Tools return compact plain text, one line per result with no field names, about 37% shorter than JSON; get takes up to 10 keys as a safety rail.
body:
Context: every response lands in the model's context, so its format is a token cost paid on every call.

Decision: plain text, one line per result, with no field names or quotes and empty fields left out. Errors are one line plus a hint. The core returns typed objects, and only the tool layer formats them. get takes a list of keys, capped by a setting (default 10), so one careless call can't dump half the graph.

Passed over: JSON, which is about 37% more characters for the same stub (the model reads, it doesn't parse). Also structured content alongside text, and an uncapped get.

Trade-offs: cheap, readable responses. A structured option can come later if a client needs it.
author: local

title: ADR 0012: Readable keys and normalization rules
summary: Keys are type/slug built from the title's words (how-to/granting-admin-access), not random ids; a live key collision stops the write, which is search-before-write built in.
body:
Context: how keys are built, and exactly what normalization means, were left open.

Decision: a key is <type>/<slug>. The slug is the title's lead clause, up to six words, lowercased, hyphenated, at most 48 characters, never ending on a filler word. If the derived key belongs to a live node, upsert stops and names it. Deleted or superseded holders get a -2 suffix, and notes always do. Node types and tags use hyphens (jira-ticket), and edge types use underscores (depends_on). A type hint fires only for a type new to the graph.

Passed over: ULID keys for notes, which cost many tokens and mean nothing to a model.

Trade-offs: keys read well everywhere. Retitling a node doesn't change its key, by design.
author: local

title: ADR 0013: Scripted benchmark method (superseded)
summary: Proposed a deterministic, scripted retrieval benchmark as the headline; superseded by ADR 0023, which takes the headline from live Claude sessions instead.
body:
Context: the headline number has to be reproducible, cheap and fair to markdown.

Proposal: fixed retrieval policies replay search then get against a shared demo dataset, and count the tokens each side reads. They're compared with whole-file, index-then-file and grep-then-file markdown strategies.

What happened: it was never accepted. Its numbers depend on how well the scripts model an agent, and it charged MCPdia every tool definition up front, which is not how Claude Code loads tools. ADR 0023 moved the headline to live sessions. The scripted bench stays as a free check of retrieval cost (npm run bench).
author: local

title: ADR 0014: Graph viewer library: Sigma.js or Cytoscape.js
summary: The viewer offers two MIT-licensed renderers: Sigma.js with graphology (WebGL, the default) and Cytoscape.js; 10k nodes load in about a second.
body:
Context: a browser viewer with clickable nodes, drill-in to neighbors, search, a type legend, hiding unrelated nodes, a permissive license, and thousands of nodes.

Decision: Sigma.js v4 with graphology (WebGL, ForceAtlas2 in a worker) as the default, and Cytoscape.js (canvas, rich layouts) as an alternative, both picked from the page. In a headless prototype, 10k nodes load in about 1 s and 50k in about 3 s.

Passed over: vis-network (slow past a few thousand nodes), force-graph (force layout only), G6 (heavy), Reagraph (React only), and cosmos.gl (thin on interaction).

Trade-offs: the viewer is a separate, optional package, so the server install stays lean. Each feature is written twice.
author: local

title: ADR 0015: Links on create, and a hint for nodes with no parent
summary: upsert takes links, so one call places a node under its parent; a new node with no parent link gets a one-line hint, never a block.
body:
Context: in real use, many nodes landed at the top level, because creating and linking took two calls and models skipped the second.

Decision: upsert takes links: [{type, to, note?}], with the same rules as link. When a new node has no parent edge (part_of, comments_on, candidate_for), the result says so in one line. It names no guess, and the write always succeeds.

Passed over: an "are you sure?" round trip, which models learn to rubber-stamp. Also guessing a parent, since a wrong link is worse than none.

Trade-offs: one call places a node where it belongs. The hint costs about 30 tokens when it fires.
author: local

title: ADR 0016: Tools say what happened
summary: When a tool knows something the caller would want (a partial match, a flagged node, a dangling link), the result says it in one line: the fact, then the next step.
body:
Context: in testing, results stayed quiet about things the server knew: a search with no full match, a node marked wrong, a delete that left links dangling, a typo in a filter that looked like an empty graph. Models acted on the wrong picture.

Decision: one-line hints that appear only when they apply and never block. search labels partial matches. get and search flag nodes marked wrong. Deleted keys say they're deleted. delete lists links left dangling. link warns about loops. upsert flags a missing summary, dropped properties or a missing parent.

Passed over: guidance in tool descriptions, which fades. Also errors, which block fine writes. Also structured warning fields, which clients may not show.

Trade-offs: a more accurate picture for a few tokens, only when something is off.
author: local

title: ADR 0017: Read and restore deleted nodes
summary: get and search take all_status to show deleted and superseded nodes, and upsert on a deleted key restores that node with its history.
body:
Context: delete was soft, but no tool could read a deleted node or reuse its key, so a delete couldn't be checked or undone.

Decision: all_status: true on get and search marks nodes (deleted) or (superseded by <key>). upsert on a deleted key restores the node: same id, same history, new version. The result says "Restored". A superseded key still refuses writes and names its replacement. Links to a restored key work again, because edges store keys.

Passed over: a fresh node on the old key, which would muddle history. Also a separate restore tool, which is one more description every session.

Trade-offs: deletes can be checked and undone with tools the model already uses.
author: local

title: ADR 0018: State facts, don't guess
summary: Results state what the server knows and where to look ("list_types shows the types in use") and never name a guess such as "did you mean ticket?".
body:
Context: string-distance guesses were sometimes wrong (restoring a node of type test suggested task), and models take a named option at face value.

Decision: hints state the fact and the place to check. Examples: 'Type "tickets" is new here. list_types shows the types in use.' and 'Not found: concept/permision. search finds nodes by their words.' Writes still never block. list_types still points out plural and separator look-alikes, because those are facts about the graph.

Passed over: tuning the distance, which is still sometimes wrong. Also dropping the new-type line, which loses the guard against drift.

Trade-offs: hints stay accurate. A typo costs one lookup call.
author: local

title: ADR 0019: Per-call metrics log
summary: An opt-in JSONL log of raw facts about each tool call (tool, ms, request and response size), next to the database; no estimates, no query text, no content.
body:
Context: Claude's usage report gives session totals. Only the server sees each tool call, so without a log a session can't be split by request.

Decision: MCPDIA_METRICS=1 turns it on, and it's off by default. Each call writes one JSON line to mcpdia-metrics.jsonl beside the database: ts, session, tool, ms, ok, req_chars, res_chars and level. One wrapper records every tool. A failed log write never fails the call. Analysis lives in the bench.

Passed over: a SQLite table plus a stats command, which was built and backed out. Also CSV, and per-call token counts, which need a network call.

Trade-offs: anyone can measure MCPdia on their own graph with one variable. The log grows until you delete it.
author: local

title: ADR 0020: Snippets show the match
summary: When a searched word sits past the first 300 characters, the search snippet shows a short intro plus the text around the match, at the same budget.
body:
Context: a snippet was the first 300 characters. In a bench session the answer started 21 characters past the cut, and the model answered from the stub without calling get.

Decision: in search, if a searched word is hidden by the cut, the snippet becomes about 100 characters of intro, then " … ", then about 200 characters around the first hidden word, ending with (+N chars). Words match the way the index does, including inside long words and URLs and with light stemming. get at snippet level keeps the plain first 300 characters.

Passed over: showing short bodies whole, and FTS5's snippet(), which picked the wrong fragment.

Trade-offs: a stub carries the fact a search word points to, at about the same cost.
author: local

title: ADR 0021: Search tops up short results with partial matches
summary: When fewer nodes match every word than the limit, the remaining places go to labelled partial matches, so one weak full hit can't hide the real answer.
body:
Context: search fell back to any-word matches only when nothing matched every word. In the bench, one stray full match ("EU workspaces AWS region") hid the node that answered, and the model reported the fact as missing.

Decision: full matches come first, then partial matches fill the remaining places, ranked by relevance and labelled with the words they matched. The header counts both kinds. The result is never more than the limit and has no repeats.

Passed over: keeping the empty-only fallback, ranking everything together, and patching the data with aliases.

Trade-offs: a short result shows the runners-up instead of empty space.
author: local

title: ADR 0022: Project name: MCPdia
summary: The project is MCPdia, short for Model Context Protocol: Distilled, Indexed Answers; the repo, npm package and runtime names all follow.
body:
Context: ADR 0009 kept the name MCPedia despite an unrelated project of the same name, to be revisited before release. Sharing a name in search results and on npm is a cost with no upside.

Decision: MCPdia, short for Model Context Protocol: Distilled, Indexed Answers. Repo bradwagoner/mcpdia, npm @bradwagoner/mcpdia, and the mcpdia command. Runtime names are MCPDIA_DB, MCPDIA_METRICS and ~/.mcpdia/mcpdia.db. There's no fallback to the old names. Older records keep the name they were written with.

Trade-offs: a distinct name. An existing graph moves by renaming one folder and one file.
author: local

title: ADR 0023: The headline comes from live sessions
summary: The README headline comes from real Claude sessions (tasks passed, dollars per session), comparing MCPdia with one CLAUDE.md and with hand-split topic files.
body:
Context: the scripted benchmark (ADR 0013) measured a model of an agent and charged every tool definition up front. Real sessions are now runnable with promptfoo and the Agent SDK.

Decision: the headline comes from bench/sessions. Each live session gets a task and a fresh copy of the same facts, kept in MCPdia, in a CLAUDE.md index with topic files, or in one CLAUDE.md. Compared on tasks passed and API-reported cost, which weighs cached tokens the way a bill does. The README states the model, the task count, the repeats and the dataset size, and links the per-session CSV. Paid runs have a cost cap.

Trade-offs: rerunning costs cents and needs an API key. Live results vary, and more repeats tighten them.
author: local

title: ADR 0024: Lookup tests without a model
summary: Accepted: free lookup checks against the real server, with no model: retrieval on 40 questions and their rewordings, render-level cost, stale facts, cost as memory grows, and scaling to 100k nodes.
body:
Status: Accepted.

Context: live sessions cost money and cover 10 tasks. They can't cheaply check, on every change, that search still finds the right node or that lookups hold up as a graph grows.

Decision: bench/lookups.ts calls the real server in memory. It runs:
- Retrieval: 40 questions, the same 40 reworded, and 10 with no answer, scored on hit@1, hit@3 and MRR.
- Tokens per render level.
- Stale-fact checks: superseded, deleted and flagged nodes never pass as current.
- Cost as memory grows from 82 to 1,600 nodes, against markdown.
- Scaling to 100,000 generated nodes.
The fast part runs on every npm test, with floors set to today's scores.

Trade-offs: search changes show their effect immediately. A same-topic worst case shows where keyword search runs out, which gives future ranking work a target.
author: local

title: ADR 0025: Postgres store, HTTP transport and a Docker image
summary: Accepted: a PostgresStore behind the same interface, a stateless Streamable HTTP transport answering localhost only, and Docker Compose that runs both with the viewer.
body:
Status: Accepted.

Context: ADR 0006 promises a team mode. Solo mode is done, and a shared contract suite was waiting for a second store. Auth is still v0.3 work, so the first image must be safe without it.

Decision:
- Store: Postgres with node-postgres. Same tables, with arrays for tags and aliases and jsonb. A weighted tsvector with English stemming and no stop words, to match SQLite. Picked by MCPDIA_DATABASE_URL.
- Transport: mcpdia --http serves stateless Streamable HTTP at /mcp on 127.0.0.1:7411 and answers only local host names, which blocks DNS rebinding. stdio stays the default.
- Docker: a two-stage node:22-slim image running as a non-root user. Compose with Postgres 17 (not published) and the viewer, both on 127.0.0.1.
- Tests: the shared suite runs on PGlite in every npm test, with no Docker needed.

Passed over: stdio inside the container (it can't serve a team), stateful sessions, and an ORM.

Trade-offs: team mode is one command. Two stores to keep in step. Until auth lands, use it on localhost or a trusted network.
author: local

title: Ways to share a graph
summary: Four ways to combine graphs: one team server, a second connector, starter sets loaded on startup, and live reads across databases. Your own notes stay private in every one.
body:
Pick by what you're sharing and how fresh it needs to be:

- One team server: everyone reads and writes one live graph. Best for a team that works together every day. Available now.
- A second connector: register a team or starter MCPdia next to your own. No code, and it works today.
- Starter sets on startup: load curated sets into their own namespaces of your graph. One search covers everything, and your notes can link to them. Edit anything; if the source also changed a node you edited, you get a conflict to review. In progress (ADR 0026).
- Live reads across databases: one server reading your graph and the team's live. Planned with team mode.

In every setup, your own graph stays yours. Shared knowledge sits beside it, never mixed in.
author: local

title: Share: one team server
summary: Everyone connects to one MCPdia server (Docker, Postgres, HTTP), so what one person's LLM learns, everyone's can find. Available now.
body:
docker compose up -d starts Postgres, the server and the live viewer. Each person registers it once:

claude mcp add --transport http mcpdia http://localhost:7411/mcp

Everyone reads and writes the same live graph. Notes are separate nodes per author, and a version check guards concurrent edits. Postgres handles many clients writing at once.

Today the server answers localhost only and has no login, so run it on one machine or a network you trust. Token auth and per-namespace permissions come with team mode (v0.3).
author: local

title: Share: a second connector
summary: Register a team or starter MCPdia server next to your own; available now with no code. The model picks which one to ask.
body:
Add a second server under its own name, pointed at another database or a shared server:

claude mcp add mcpdia-team -e MCPDIA_DB=/path/team.db -- node /path/mcpdia/dist/index.js
claude mcp add --transport http mcpdia-team http://host:7411/mcp

Your private graph stays on your own server. The team's knowledge comes from the other.

Trade-offs:
- The model picks which server to ask, using tool names such as mcp__mcpdia__search and mcp__mcpdia-team__search.
- Two tool lists. In Claude Code they're deferred, about 260 tokens each until used.
- Results from the two never rank together, and notes can't link across.
author: local

title: Share: starter sets loaded on startup
summary: Curated sets load into their own namespaces of your graph at startup: one search, links across, fresh at each start. Edit anything; if the source also changed it, you get a conflict to review (ADR 0026).
body:
MCPDIA_STARTERS=mcpdia=./starters/mcpdia.jsonl,team=http://localhost:7411/export

Each set loads into the namespace named before the =. It can come from a file or from another MCPdia server's export. Then:

- One search ranks your notes and the starter sets together.
- Your notes can link to mcpdia:concept/stubs-first.
- Edit anything. Nodes you haven't touched follow the source; nodes you edited stay yours.
- If the source also changed a node you edited, you get one conflict node to review. It's listed when the set loads and marked on the node in get and search ("newer version in mcpdia:conflict/..."). The resolve-conflicts prompt walks through them. Once resolved, a conflict stays resolved until the source changes that node again.
- A set that hasn't changed is skipped at start. If a source is unreachable, the server starts with the copy it loaded last time.

You make a set with mcpdia export --tag <tag>. It works like a package install that keeps your local changes: fresh as of each start. For edits that show up mid-session, connect to the team server directly.
author: local

title: Share: live reads across databases
summary: One server reading your database and the team's live, always current, with one search across both. Planned with team mode (v0.3).
body:
Your server would read your own graph and the team's graph live, merging search results across both, with your writes staying in yours. It needs search merging across stores and credentials for the other database, so it arrives with team mode, alongside token auth and per-namespace permissions.

Until then, starter sets give you one search and links across, and a team server or a second connector gives you live edits.
author: local

title: ADR 0026: Starter sets loaded on startup
summary: The server loads starter sets (files or URLs) into their own namespaces at startup, next to your graph. Edit anything; when the source also changed a node you edited, the load writes one conflict node to review.
body:
Context: a graph is more useful when it can lean on knowledge someone else keeps, such as a starter set or a team's notes, while your own notes stay yours. A copy raises one question: what happens when you edit a node and the source changes it too?

Decision:
- MCPDIA_STARTERS=name=path-or-url,... loads each set into its own namespace. Relative paths are read from the database's folder. Sources are read in parallel, with a 5-second URL timeout and a 50 MB cap. BOM and UTF-16 files are accepted. MCPDIA_NAMESPACES adds other read namespaces, and MCPDIA_WRITE_NAMESPACE picks where new nodes go. A starter namespace can't be the write namespace.
- Starter nodes are editable. Each reload does a three-way check per key: base (last applied or acknowledged), yours and incoming, hashed on content and status.
  - Untouched nodes follow the source, and your edits stay.
  - Both changed: one conflict node. Gone upstream but edited: a conflict saying it was removed.
  - Nodes you add to a starter namespace are never touched. A first load refuses a namespace holding other nodes.
  - Links the set wrote follow the source, and yours stay.
- Conflict: conflict/<node key> (e.g. conflict/concept/stubs-first) in the starter namespace, holding the incoming version, with conflicts_with to your node. It's updated in place for newer versions. Deleting it marks that version handled, and a later change reopens it. Nothing resolves itself.
- Conflicts are listed at load (startup stderr, seed output) and marked in get and search. The resolve-conflicts prompt walks through them.
- An unchanged source is skipped. An unreachable one keeps the last copy.
- Making a set: export with no namespace named covers your write namespace only, so loaded sets are never passed along. Someone who wants the same set lists it under the same name, so links into it resolve. A file repeating a key is refused. Use mcpdia export --tag <tag>, or GET /export. A one-off load: mcpdia seed <file> --namespace <ns>.

Passed over: read-only sets (frustrating), copy-on-edit (two nodes per key), one conflict per version (piles up, can hide newer ones), and deleting rows to reload (breaks no-hard-delete).

Trade-offs: your edits survive reloads. A node you edited stops following the source until you take its version. The set list is fixed at startup. Merge import (v0.2) can reuse the conflict nodes.
author: local
